result: Virtual 3D objects globally enhanced hippocampal spatial coding resolution. The proportion of place cells increased from 19% to 71% in the presence of objects (C39-C40), with fields concentrated in the central track (C42). Objects improved place field stability (C46: p<10⁻¹⁰), reduced spatial dispersion (C45: p=0.01), decreased out-of-field firing (C49: p<10⁻⁷), and increased spatial information content (C50: p<10⁻⁷).
evaluation: Multiple converging measures with strong statistical significance demonstrate that 3D objects enhance spatial coding. The claims are internally consistent, with appropriate statistical tests (WRS, t-tests) and clear effect sizes. Sample sizes are adequate (n=3 mice per condition, 48-193 place cells), and the findings align across different metrics of spatial coding quality.

result: Virtual 3D objects locally enhanced spatial coding resolution in their vicinity (Object Zones, OZ). Place field density was significantly higher in OZ versus ØZ (C53: p=0.002), with smaller field widths (C54: p<10⁻⁵), reduced dispersion (C55: p<10⁻⁴), increased local stability (C56: p<10⁻⁶), and higher spatial information (C57: p=0.03). The out-of-field firing ratio effect was more global (C58, C60).
evaluation: The local analysis demonstrates spatial specificity of object effects with strong statistical support. The distinction between local effects (field density, size, stability) and global effects (out-of-field firing) is well-documented. The spatial binning approach (2-10 cm bins) is appropriate for the 2m track, and the non-uniform distribution test (C52: p=0.017) validates the spatial clustering.

result: Overrepresentation of place fields at track ends in ØT was not associated with increased spatial coding resolution. End-track fields showed no improvement in out-of-field firing ratio (C62: p=0.83), stability (C63: p=0.26), and paradoxically lower spatial information than on-track fields (C64: p=0.008).
evaluation: This negative result is important for distinguishing overrepresentation from increased coding resolution. The statistical comparisons are appropriate, and the finding that end-track fields have lower spatial information despite higher density argues against reward-related enhancement of spatial coding in this paradigm.

result: Population-level decoding analysis confirmed that objects improved spatial coding accuracy both globally and locally. Decoding error was nearly two-fold larger without objects (C66: p<10⁻³⁶), and decoding accuracy was three-fold lower (C67: p<10⁻⁵⁴). Local analysis showed significantly better decoding in OZ versus ØZ (C71: p<10⁻⁶), even when using fewer cells from OT than ØT (C69).
evaluation: The Bayesian decoding analysis provides strong population-level validation of single-cell findings. The drop-cell approach (C68-C69) controls for differences in place cell proportions, strengthening the conclusion. The 150ms time windows and leave-one-out cross-validation are appropriate methodological choices. Convergence with FRV decoding method adds robustness.

result: Object manipulations produced rapid, dynamic changes in spatial coding resolution. Adding objects instantaneously increased place cell proportion from 21.6% to 75.0% (C74: p<10⁻⁵), with 40.3% of cells becoming spatially modulated (C75). Removing objects reversed these effects (C83-C85). Map similarity analysis showed changes stabilized by the second trial after adding objects (C88) and immediately after removing objects (C89).
evaluation: The manipulation experiments provide strong causal evidence for object effects on spatial coding. The rapid timescale (1-2 trials) distinguishes these effects from slower learning-related changes. The bidirectional manipulation (adding and removing objects) strengthens causal inference. Sample sizes are adequate (n=5 and n=8 sessions for adding/removing), and statistical tests are appropriate (paired t-tests for within-session comparisons).

result: 2D wall patterns (PØT) provided intermediate enhancement of spatial coding between ØT and OT. Place cell proportion in PØT (42.16%) was between ØT (18.71%) and OT (71.11%), with uniform field distribution (C98: p=0.23). Stability, spatial information, and local decoding accuracy in PØT were significantly better than ØT but worse than OT (C102, C105, C107-C108).
evaluation: The graded effect across three conditions (ØT < PØT < OT) supports the hypothesis that local visual cue quality/dimensionality affects spatial coding resolution. The uniform distribution in PØT versus clustered distribution in OT suggests 2D cues can set field positions but 3D cues provide additional local enhancement. Statistical comparisons use appropriate post-hoc corrections (Bonferroni) for multiple comparisons.

result: Visual enrichment (EOT) did not further improve spatial coding beyond OT. Place cell proportions and field attributes were not significantly different between OT and EOT (C109-C110, C113). However, field distribution became uniform in EOT (C111), and objects still locally improved stability and decoding accuracy in OZ versus ØZ (C114-C115).
evaluation: This result suggests a ceiling effect for spatial coding enhancement, where additional distal visual cues provide diminishing returns once local 3D objects are present. The persistent local effect of objects in EOT (C114-C115) despite uniform field distribution indicates objects influence both field placement and local coding quality. The lack of differences in most metrics (C113) is well-supported statistically.

result: Local visual cues were essential for theta phase precession. In OT, 40.22% of fields showed significant phase precession with negative correlation (r=-0.14±0.018, p<10⁻¹⁴) and slopes (-2.00±0.17 rad/U, p<10⁻¹⁴). In ØT, only 7.46% of fields precessed (p<10⁻⁶ vs OT), with no significant phase-position correlation (C130: p=0.30). Theta frequency, power, and spike coupling were not significantly different between conditions (C121-C122, C126-C128).
evaluation: The theta phase precession analysis is rigorous, using spatially stable trials in ØT to control for stability differences. Multiple analysis methods (Hilbert transform, waveform-based, single-trial) converge on the same conclusion. The lack of differences in basic theta properties (C121-C128) rules out confounding explanations. The unit-LFP shift analysis provides independent confirmation. Sample sizes are adequate (177 fields in OT, 15 in ØT for SST).

result: Local visual cues enabled theta timescale spike coordination. Strong correlation between theta phase and physical distance was observed in OT (R=0.39, n=629 pairs, p<10⁻²⁴) but not ØT (R=0.21, n=28 pairs, p=0.26). This demonstrates that local cues are important for temporal coding beyond phase precession.
evaluation: The theta sequence analysis examines spike timing relationships between cell pairs with overlapping place fields, providing a population-level measure of temporal coding. The strong correlation in OT and lack thereof in ØT is well-supported statistically. However, the small number of pairs in ØT (n=28) reflects the low proportion of place cells in that condition, which could limit power for detecting weaker effects.

result: The experimental setup used head-fixed mice running on a wheel in a 2m virtual linear track with distinct wall patterns and reward zones at extremities. Mice performed similarly in ØT and OT conditions (reward rate: p=0.59; running speed: p=0.64). A total of 1021 neurons were recorded from CA1, with comparable proportions of active cells between conditions (p=0.14).
evaluation: The experimental design is well-described and appropriate for the research question. The virtual reality setup allows precise control of visual cues while maintaining behavioral engagement. Similar task performance between conditions (C36-C37) rules out motivation or attention differences as confounds. The comparable proportion of active cells (C38) indicates objects don't simply increase overall excitability. Sample sizes (n=3 mice per condition, 1021 total neurons) are adequate for the analyses performed.

result: Object-responsive (OR) cells, which fire near multiple objects, were rare in this study. No OR cells were detected in ØT, and only 2.07% of place cells in OT were classified as OR cells. This indicates that the majority of newly activated place cells in OT do not correspond to OR cells.
evaluation: The OR cell analysis addresses an important alternative explanation for increased place cell numbers near objects. The low proportion (2.07%) is consistent with previous literature reporting 6-8% in dorsal hippocampus. The classification criteria (bidirectional firing near same objects) are appropriate. However, the analysis could be limited by the specific definition used and the virtual nature of the objects.

result: The introduction establishes that flexible navigation relies on hippocampal cognitive maps (C1), with place cells providing the neural substrate (C9-C10). Dynamic control of spatial coding resolution could be important for navigation (C11), as mapping all space at high resolution would be computationally expensive (C13). Previous work shows place cell coding varies with behavioral conditions (C15-C16) and that local sensory cues could be instrumental in setting spatial coding resolution (C26).
evaluation: These claims provide appropriate background and motivation for the study. They are well-supported by citations to foundational and recent literature. The logical progression from established knowledge (C1, C9-C10) through computational considerations (C13) to the specific hypothesis (C26) is clear and well-justified. These are primarily literature review claims that set up the experimental work.

result: The discussion synthesizes findings and contextualizes them within existing literature. Key points include: (1) local visual cues dramatically increased place cell numbers (threefold), exceeding predictions from previous studies with real objects (C139-C143); (2) the effects are more compatible with improved spatial coding resolution than object-responsive cell activation (C155-C156); (3) overrepresentation can be dissociated from increased coding resolution (C157-C160); (4) the results complement previous VR studies showing distal cues alone are insufficient (C162-C163).
evaluation: The discussion appropriately interprets the findings in light of previous work. The comparison with Burke et al. 2011 (C149-C152) is particularly insightful, noting that while both studies found increased place cells with objects, the current study shows local increases in place cell density despite smaller fields. The acknowledgment of limitations (virtual vs. real objects, C153-C154) is appropriate. The mechanistic speculation is reasonable but clearly identified as such.

result: The discussion proposes several mechanisms for how objects improve spatial coding: (1) objects as stable reference points for path integration (C164-C165); (2) higher sensory resolution of local cues (C166-C167); (3) attentional modulation (C169), though task performance was similar between conditions (C170); (4) objects as noise is ruled out by poor decoding in ØT (C171-C172). For temporal coding, the discussion notes that phase precession was reduced without local cues (C173) but restored with objects (C174), and that the relationship between theta-speed modulation and phase precession is complex (C183-C185).
evaluation: The mechanistic discussion is appropriately speculative while being grounded in the data and previous literature. The ruling out of the noise hypothesis (C171-C172) is data-driven. The comparison with Ravassard et al. 2013 regarding theta-speed modulation (C183-C184) appropriately acknowledges complexity rather than forcing a simple interpretation. The discussion of phase precession mechanisms is cautious, noting that "future studies are needed" rather than overinterpreting the current findings.

result: The discussion concludes that local visual cues induce both global and local rescaling of spatial coding (C190), which could be computationally beneficial for large-scale navigation (C191-C195). In the wild, rodents travel long distances through varied terrain (C191), and mapping everything at high resolution would be costly (C192). The ability to map important locations at high resolution while using lower resolution for transit routes could be advantageous (C195), with resolution depending on local sensory information (C196).
evaluation: This functional interpretation is reasonable speculation based on the findings. The computational argument (C192-C195) is logical and supported by citations. The connection to natural behavior (C191) provides ecological validity. However, the study doesn't directly test navigational accuracy or memory, so the functional benefits remain hypothetical. The claim appropriately uses conditional language ("could be") rather than asserting proven benefits.
